summary:
Planetary Analog Finder scores 33 Earth sites against eight specific targets on the Moon and Mars — including Shackleton crater rim and Jezero Crater — using open NASA, ESA and NOAA data.

The challenge asks which Earth locations are useful analogs and where the analogy breaks down. Most comparisons collapse into a single number. Ours never does: terrain, temperature swing, surface brightness and dust are scored separately, each with its data coverage and confidence, and gravity, atmosphere and radiation are listed as not comparable at all. Users set what matters for their mission and the ranking updates live.

We also screened 1.2 million land cells worldwide. One top-ranking region sits 16 km from Black Point Lava Flow, where NASA and JAXA run Artemis rover trials — a site the scoring engine is structurally forbidden to read until after ranking is complete.

This matters because analog sites are chosen by history and access rather than measurement, and field campaigns are expensive. It also matters because of what failed: four comparison methods were withdrawn after we found the instruments were measuring different physical quantities that share a name. We report those alongside the results.
details:
Planetary Analog Finder

What it does

Earth is where we rehearse for the Moon and Mars — rovers tested in deserts, drills in volcanic ash. These are analog sites, and they have mostly been chosen by history and access rather than measurement. The same handful repeats: the Atacama, the Antarctic Dry Valleys, Iceland, Hawaii.

Planetary Analog Finder scores Earth locations against specific places on the Moon and Mars using open orbital data, and shows exactly where each comparison holds and where it breaks down.

How it works

We describe each target with numbers. Eight targets: four lunar — a mare plain, a polar region, Shackleton crater rim and Malapert massif, the last two real candidates for a permanent outpost — and four Martian: Jezero, Nili Patera, Oxia Planum and Gale. Profiles come from orbital instruments and store a range, not just an average, so we know what variation actually exists there.

We measure 33 Earth sites the same way, from open NASA, ESA and NOAA archives.

We score each dimension separately and never merge them into a single headline number. Terrain, temperature swing, surface brightness and dust each carry their own score, a data-coverage percentage and a confidence tier. A marker flags the weakest individual measurement inside each dimension, so a reasonable-looking average cannot conceal a severe mismatch. Weight sliders let a user change what matters for their mission; the ranking updates live, because how to weight dimensions is a judgment and we would rather expose that than pretend it is a fact.

We state plainly what cannot be compared at all. Gravity, atmosphere, radiation and absolute temperature are listed as not comparable and never scored.

We searched the whole planet — 1.2 million land cells scored against two Martian targets at 5.5 km resolution, then clustered into regions.

What we found

Not everything worked, and the failures are reported alongside the results.

No Earth site is a lunar thermal analog: thermal similarity is uniformly low against a 292 K diurnal swing, so it carries 47% of the lunar weighting while discriminating almost nothing. Broadband surface brightness cannot separate dark vegetation from dark basalt — a forest site matched lunar mare until we hardened the vegetation gate. Our snow filter, applied so that brightness and temperature stay physically valid, excluded polar cold deserts, which are among Earth's closest Martian environments.

Four comparison methods were withdrawn during development. Three failed for the same underlying reason: the two instruments measured different physical quantities that share a name — lunar "normal albedo" against Earth "broadband albedo", a spectral feature's wavelength position against a spectral contrast, a dimensionless index against a modelled SI quantity. Units can be converted and calibration handled statistically; a quantity mismatch cannot be repaired by any transformation, and it is easy to miss. We document all three.

One result stands out. Our global screen surfaced a region in northern Arizona, 16 km from Black Point Lava Flow — where NASA and JAXA run Desert RATS Artemis rover trials — and about 40 km from Meteor Crater, where Apollo astronauts trained. Separately, our site-level scoring gave Black Point 0.97 terrain similarity against the Apollo 11 mare region. NASA quarries its JSC-1A lunar soil simulant from the same volcanic field. None of this was an input: the documented-analog list is structurally forbidden from the scoring path, enforced by an automated repository test.

Benefits and impact

Analog campaigns are expensive and logistics-driven. A measurement-based ranking gives planners an argument for a different site, on the specific property their test depends on. Materials researchers sourcing simulant get the planet ranked on the properties that actually matter. And by publishing what we could not compare, we offer a checklist other cross-planetary comparison work can reuse.

Tools

Python 3.11 with numpy, pandas, scipy and scikit-learn; rasterio, h5py, pyhdf and astropy for raster, HDF and FITS products; Streamlit, folium and plotly for the interface. Everything runs on a laptop — no GPU, no paid cloud.

Data from NASA (MODIS, ASTER GED, LRO LOLA and Diviner, MOLA, TES, THEMIS, GIBS), ESA (Copernicus GLO-30, Sentinel-2), NOAA (ETOPO1), USGS, the European Commission (JRC Global Surface Water) and the Mars Climate Database consortium.

What makes it creative

We built a comparability framework rather than a similarity score. Every feature is classed by whether it can be compared directly, compared after a documented transformation, or not at all — and the third class is displayed as prominently as the first. The project treats its own failures as results. We also measured a cross-planetary process, not just static properties: dune migration at White Sands from Sentinel-2 imagery, compared against published Martian sand-flux rates.

Factors we considered

Resolution matching — Earth elevation is resampled to the planetary grid before computing slope, because roughness is scale-dependent. Missing data is handled by redistributing weights, never by imputing a value. Normalisation ranges are fixed and documented, so adding a site cannot silently change every other score. Confidence is reported separately from similarity. And every number traces to its source dataset, query, retrieval date and whether it was measured, derived, taken from literature or assigned by judgment.
